items.title: The subobject inequalities underlying exactness
items.strategy: Factor f as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism m. The implication gf = 0 forces m to factor through ker g, while the converse is immediate from the kernel universal property; the dual inequality is then exactly the universal factorization condition through m.

items.title: Exactness at a node
The arrow-theoretic criterion for exactness
items.strategy: Translate im(f) = ker(g) into the statement that gf = 0 and that the kernel inclusion of g is also the cokernel kernel comparison for f. The reverse direction packages the two arrow equalities back into the image-kernel comparison from item 1.

items.title: Exact sequence and short exact sequence in an abelian category
A short exact sequence is a kernel-cokernel pair
items.strategy: Use the endpoint zero objects to read short exactness through the arrow criterion at $A$ and $C$, then use the middle-node exactness equalities to identify $i$ with $\ker(p)$ and $p$ with $\operatorname{coker}(i)$.

items.title: Degenerate exactness criteria
items.strategy: Read one-sided exactness through exactness at a node: claim 1 is the zero-kernel characterization, claim 2 identifies a monic map with the kernel subobject of the next arrow, and claim 3 is the dual quotient statement. Combine those one-sided criteria to recover the short exact case.

items.title: Exactness is self-dual
items.strategy: Pass the defining equality im(f) = ker(g) to the opposite category, where image and coimage as well as kernel and cokernel are interchanged. The opposite of an abelian category is abelian, so the same definition applies on both sides.

items.title: Split short exact sequence in an abelian category
Splitting lemma in an abelian category
items.strategy: Starting from a section or retraction, use the kernel-cokernel description of a short exact sequence to construct the missing projection or section. The biproduct equations then show the five-tuple is a direct sum, and uniqueness follows by composing with the defining injections and projections.

items.title: FALSE: a short exact sequence splits whenever its middle object is isomorphic to the biproduct of the outer two
items.strategy: Refute the statement with the stabilized nonsplit extension over k[eps]/(eps^2) described in the design notes. The point of the witness is that an abstract isomorphism of objects does not supply the compatible section or retraction demanded by item 9.

items.title: Member of an object
Equivalence of members
Member equivalence is reflexive and symmetric
items.strategy: Reflexivity uses the identity epimorphism on the member domain, and symmetry just swaps the two comparison maps. The point of separating this from item 14 is to isolate the sole nonformal use of abelian exactness there.

items.title: Member equivalence is transitive
items.strategy: Given xu = yv and yw = zr with u, v, w, r epic, form the pullback of v and w. The induced legs remain epic by the pullback-of-an-epi theorem, and the two comparison equations then exhibit x and z as equivalent over the pullback object.

items.title: Members modulo equivalence correspond to subobjects
items.strategy: Factor each member through its epi-mono factorization and assign to it the represented subobject. Equivalent members have mutually factoring monic parts, while every subobject is represented by its own monomorphism viewed as a member.

items.title: Each object has a zero member and each member has a negative
items.strategy: The zero arrow into an object is a member, and the additive inverse of any arrow gives the negative member. If x is equivalent to zero, then cancel the witnessing epimorphism to conclude that x itself is the zero arrow.

items.title: A morphism carries members to members and preserves equivalence
items.strategy: Postcompose the representative arrows with the morphism. Any witnessing pair of epimorphisms for x equiv y still witnesses fx equiv fy because the defining square remains commutative after composition.

items.title: Monicity is detected by members
items.strategy: If f is monic and fx is equivalent to zero, cancel the common comparison to show x is zero. Conversely, test the stated property on the member given by the equalizer of a parallel pair to recover left cancellability.

items.title: Monicity by member cancellation
items.strategy: Apply item 18 to the difference of two members after transporting them to a common domain. The reverse implication is immediate by setting one member to zero.

items.title: Epimorphy is detected by members
items.strategy: Translate the existence of a preimage member for every member of the codomain into the statement that every member-subobject of the codomain lies in im(g). By item 15, that means the image subobject is the whole codomain, hence g is epic.

items.title: A zero arrow is detected by members
items.strategy: One direction is immediate from preservation of equivalence. For the converse, apply the hypothesis to the identity member 1_r : r -> r and use item 16 to convert equivalence to the zero member into literal equality of arrows.

items.title: Exactness is detected by members
items.strategy: Use item 15 to identify a member y of b with the subobject represented by its image. The condition gy equiv 0 means that subobject lies in ker g, and the existence of x with fx equiv y says the same subobject lies in im f; item 1 then converts this to exactness.

items.title: The subtraction surrogate
items.strategy: Choose a common epic comparison domain with gxu = gyv, and define z = yv - xu on that domain. Then gz = 0 by additivity, and the two moreover clauses come from substituting z into any morphism that already kills x or y.

items.title: What the subtraction rule does not say
items.strategy: Record the three failure modes the designer called out: z is not unique, members have no ambient subtraction law, and the rule constrains z only through morphisms already killing x or y. The remark exists to stop later pages from silently reintroducing element arithmetic.

items.title: The members of an object do not form a group
items.strategy: Work in Ab and use the identity member of Z. Item 16 shows every member is equivalent to its negative, but 2 * 1_Z is not equivalent to zero, so no group law on equivalence classes can be inferred from the ambient additive structure on arrows.

items.title: Two morphisms agreeing on every member need not be equal
items.strategy: Again in Ab, compare 1_Z and -1_Z. Every member x : X -> Z is equivalent to -x after precomposition with -1_X, but the two endomorphisms of Z are distinct, so memberwise agreement is weaker than equality.

items.title: The cost of the member calculus
items.strategy: State the exact proof inputs honestly: finite limits and colimits together with the pullback-of-an-epi theorem from MA-8. The remark also records what is not used and avoids the unsupported stronger claim that the method is constructive.

items.title: A square is cartesian exactly when a short sequence is exact
items.strategy: Encode a commutative square over f and g as the kernel diagram of (f, -g) on the biproduct X oplus Y. The pullback universal property and the kernel universal property are then the same statement, with the sign needed to express commutativity as vanishing.

items.title: A cartesian square induces an isomorphism on the kernels of its parallel legs
items.strategy: Apply the published kernel-isomorphism theorem to a pullback square, or rederive it from item 28 by comparing the two short exact sequences attached to the square. This is the exact-sequence form later diagram chases quote.

items.title: A cartesian square over an epimorphism is also cocartesian
items.strategy: Use item 28 to identify the square with a short exact sequence on the left, then use epicity of the parallel leg to make the right-hand comparison map a cokernel as well. This recovers the pushout statement without leaving the exact-sequence language.

items.title: Epimorphisms in an abelian category are universal
items.strategy: This is the pullback stability of epimorphisms from MA-8, restated as a named property because items 28, 30, 32, and the next page cite it as such.

items.title: The covering criterion for exactness
items.strategy: Translate exactness into the member criterion, keeping the composite-zero condition $gf=0$ explicit. One direction turns a member lift $fx \equiv h$ into an actual lift after a common epic refinement, and the converse converts such refined lifts back into the member criterion.

items.title: The covering criterion and the member calculus are the same tool
items.strategy: Record explicitly that a member is an arrow into the object and that equivalence of members is agreement after precomposition by epimorphisms. This identifies item 32 with item 22 stripped of notation and licenses both idioms on the next page.

items.title: The kernel row and cokernel row of a morphism of short exact sequences are exact at two nodes each
items.strategy: Build the relevant pullback squares from the morphism of short exact sequences and use items 28 and 29 to read off the first two exact nodes in the kernel row. The cokernel row follows by duality through item 7.

items.title: The kernel row of a morphism of short exact sequences need not be short exact
items.strategy: Compute the kernel row for the vertical morphism (2, 2, 0) on two copies of 0 -> Z -> Z -> Z/2 -> 0. The first two exactness nodes survive as item 34 predicts, but the last arrow is not epic and the snake connecting morphism is the missing Z/2 -> Z/2 isomorphism.

items.title: Exactness of kernel and cokernel sequences under endpoint hypotheses
items.strategy: Apply the covering criterion to the kernel sequence in the presence of a monic left endpoint, and dualize for the cokernel sequence when the right endpoint is epic. The statement is kept with all letters displayed because later diagram-lemma proofs cite it by shape.

items.title: The kernel-cokernel sequence of a composite
items.strategy: Apply item 36 to the natural morphism between the two short exact sequences attached to f and gf, and then to gf and g. Splicing the resulting exact rows produces the six-term exact sequence for the composite.

items.title: Comember and the dual calculus
Two routes to every dual statement
items.strategy: Record that one may either dualize a member argument through item 7 or run the comember calculus directly. The remark exists so the next page can cite a deliberate choice rather than silently swap methods mid-proof.

items.title: Hom is left exact in each variable
items.strategy: Representable functors preserve all existing small limits, hence kernels. Therefore a short left exact sequence stays left exact after applying Hom(x, -); the contravariant variable follows by passing to the opposite abelian category.

items.title: Hom is not exact
items.strategy: Reuse the standard sequence 0 -> Z -> Z -> Z/2 -> 0 as a concrete short exact sequence in Ab and apply Hom_Z(-, Z) inside the abelian-category setting. The example keeps the same witness as the published module counterexample, but does not depend on a B-page item from another page.

items.title: An object is projective exactly when Hom out of it is exact
items.strategy: Combine the lifting characterization of projective objects with item 40 to upgrade left exactness to exactness precisely when epimorphisms are sent to surjections. The injective half is the dual statement in the opposite category.

items.title: AB5 is equivalent to exactness of filtered colimits
items.strategy: Use the AB5 lattice law to control kernels in filtered short exact diagrams. For the converse, view the intersections $B_i \wedge C$ as a filtered diagram of pullbacks and use exactness of filtered colimits to preserve that pullback square, identifying the resulting images with $\bigvee_i(B_i \wedge C)$ and $(\bigvee_i B_i)\wedge C$.

items.title: FALSE: two morphisms that agree on every member are equal
items.strategy: Item 26 is the direct refutation. Item 21 remains the only legitimate member-based equality test, and only against zero.

items.title: FALSE: the members of an object form an abelian group
items.strategy: Item 25 supplies the witness in Ab. The failure is structural: the subtraction surrogate of item 23 is weaker than a binary operation on member classes.

items.title: FALSE: member equivalence is transitive in any pointed category with pullbacks
items.strategy: Refute the statement by pointing back to item 14: the proof spends the pullback stability of epimorphisms, not just the existence of pullbacks. The false statement exists so later authoring cannot quietly weaken that hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: the kernel row of a morphism of short exact sequences is short exact
items.strategy: Item 35 gives the explicit multiplication-by-two witness. The positive theorem is only the two-node exactness of item 34, and the missing third exactness is exactly what the snake lemma repairs on the next page.

items.title: FALSE: the subtraction rule produces a unique member
items.strategy: Work in $\mathbf{Ab}$ with $B=\mathbb Z$, $C=0$, $g=0$, and $x=y=0$. Both $0_{\mathbb Z}$ and $1_{\mathbb Z}$ satisfy $gz \equiv 0$, so the subtraction surrogate witness is not unique.

items.title: FALSE: the subobject-side definition of exactness needs no canonical image monomorphism
items.strategy: Item 1 is the refutation: the comparison im(f) -> ker(g) is not ambient data but must be constructed from gf = 0. Without that arrow there is no well-typed equality of subobjects to call exactness.

title: Exactness and the Member Calculus — Examples

items.title: Members of an abelian group correspond to its subgroups
items.strategy: Identify a member x : X -> A with its image subgroup im(x) in the ordinary sense, and compare member equivalence with equality of image subgroups. This is the concrete Ab instance of item 15.

items.title: An ordinary element as the member from the integers
items.strategy: For an abelian group A and element a in A, view a as the morphism Z -> A sending 1 to a. The example shows how ordinary elements embed into the member formalism without exhausting it.

items.title: A general member of an abelian group need not come from an element
items.strategy: Use the identity morphism of Z^2 as a member of Z^2. Its image is noncyclic, so it cannot factor through Z and therefore cannot arise from a single ordinary element.

items.title: A member chase verifying monicity
items.strategy: Choose a familiar monomorphism of abelian groups, run rule (i) or (ii) on explicit members, and show how the argument mirrors an element chase while remaining phrased in morphisms and equivalence classes.

items.title: The covering criterion checked in abelian groups
items.strategy: Take a short exact sequence of abelian groups and verify item 32 directly on a concrete map h into the middle term. The example makes the epimorphic cover v -> w completely explicit.

items.title: The kernel-cokernel sequence of a composite of module maps
items.strategy: Pick concrete module maps f and g, compute the kernels and cokernels of f, g, and gf, and check the six-term exact sequence from item 37 by hand.

items.title: A non-split short exact sequence of abelian groups
items.strategy: Reuse the standard sequence 0 -> Z -> Z -> Z/2 -> 0 as a concrete short exact sequence in Ab and verify directly that no section of the quotient can exist. This exhibits the categorical split-sequence notion on a familiar nonsplit extension without depending on a B-page item from another page.

items.title: The splitting lemma instantiated at the published module theorem
items.strategy: Match the categorical statement of item 9 to the already-published module splitting lemma and check that the section, retraction, and biproduct data line up literally.

items.title: The kernel row failure for multiplication by two computed
items.strategy: Work through the exact same diagram used in item 35 and compute every kernel and connecting morphism explicitly. The example makes the failure of short exactness visible before the snake lemma repairs it.
